problem: Standard deep RL policies (DQN, A3C) map state to action with the goal baked into the network weights, so every new navigation target needs a fully retrained model. They are also very data-inefficient, and there was no photo-realistic, interactive 3D simulator in which to train and evaluate visual navigation at scale; ATARI, ViZDoom and SceneNet are either 2D, non-photorealistic, or not interactive.
motivation: Training DRL on a real robot for every possible target is prohibitive, and real-world goals are effectively countless. The authors note that training episodes for different targets share information: common routes and scene regularities (e.g., a fridge is near a microwave). A policy conditioned on the goal, trained on many targets at once in realistic simulated scenes, should therefore learn faster and transfer to new targets, new scenes and real images.
key_idea: Make the policy a function of both the current observation and a target image. A siamese actor-critic network embeds both into a shared space, and scene-specific heads sit on top. The network is trained with A3C-style asynchronous threads, each thread chasing a different target, in the new photo-realistic AI2-THOR simulator.
insight: Conditioning on the goal and sharing weights across targets and threads mainly buys data efficiency. After 100M frames the final model needs 210.7 steps on average, versus 723.5 for A3C with 4 threads and 2539.2 for One-step Q. The scene-specific heads matter: removing them (single branch) raises this to 581.6 steps, and a single-branch model applied to new scenes without fine-tuning does worse than chance. t-SNE of the learned observation embeddings shows spatial layout is preserved: pairwise embedding distance correlates with scene-coordinate distance at Pearson 0.62, p<0.001. This suggests the model implicitly learns a rough map and localizes itself in it. Generalization to unseen targets rises with the number of trained targets and with how close new targets are to trained ones, so the transfer is mostly local.
method: AI2-THOR framework: Unity3D physics engine connected directly to TensorFlow. It has 32 artist-built photo-realistic indoor scenes (kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom), about 68 object instances per scene, and supports physical and object-state interactions.

Task formulation: the goal is an RGB image taken at the target location and viewpoint. The stochastic policy π(s_t, g | u) is conditioned on both the current observation s_t and the target image g. Reward is +10.0 on reaching the goal and a -0.01 time penalty per step.

Generic siamese layers: a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 produces 2048-d features for each 224×224 RGB image; the state stacks 4 history frames. Weight-shared FC layers project both streams to 512-d, and a fusion FC takes the 1024-d concatenation to a 512-d joint embedding.

Scene-specific layers: a separate branch per scene with two FC layers outputs 4 action probabilities (policy) and 1 value (critic). All targets in a scene share its branch; all scenes share the generic layers.

Training: A3C-style asynchronous advantage actor-critic with 100 threads, each assigned a different navigation target. Uses a shared RMSProp optimizer (lr 7×10^-4) for 100M frames, taking about 1.25 h per 1M frames on one Titan X.

Action space: forward/backward 0.5 m and turn left/right 90°, with Gaussian noise N(0,0.01) on steps and N(0,1.0) on turns; this is effectively a grid world. A continuous-physics variant lets the physics engine handle collisions.

Transfer: for a new scene, the generic siamese layers are frozen and only the scene-specific layers are trained. For the real robot, simulation-trained generic layers are transferred and either frozen or fine-tuned on real images.

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (ImageNet-pretrained, frozen) + siamese FC embedding + scene-specific actor-critic heads (trained from scratch with A3C-style RL)
setting.training_data: RL in AI2-THOR: 100 targets sampled from 20 indoor scenes, 100M training frames across 100 threads. Generalization experiments use 20M frames (target transfer, 10 largest scenes) and 1–16 training scenes (scene transfer). Real-robot fine-tuning uses real RGB images at 28 discrete locations × 4 orientations.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (224×224, 4 stacked history frames) + RGB goal image
setting.action_space: 4 discrete actions: move forward/backward 0.5 m, turn left/right 90° (with Gaussian noise); grid-world discretization (continuous-physics variant also tested)
setting.privileged: scene identity at test time (selects the scene-specific branch); main evaluation targets are the same targets seen in training; no map/pose used by the policy (map used only for the shortest-path upper bound)

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 goals randomly sampled from 20 AI2-THOR scenes (the same targets used in training), 10 episodes per target from random starts; episode capped at 10,000 steps

numbers_note: Only Table I gives numeric navigation results. Target generalization (Fig. 7, success rate = trajectories shorter than 500 steps, versus number of trained targets and distance to them) and scene generalization (Fig. 8, learning curves) are shown only as figures. The real-robot result is reported only as '44% faster' convergence than training from scratch. No standard benchmark or SR/SPL metrics are used.
results: After 100M frames the full target-driven siamese model reaches targets in 210.7 steps on average, against a 17.6-step shortest-path upper bound. The strongest baseline, A3C with 4 threads per target, needs 723.5 steps; A3C with 1 thread needs 1241.3, One-step Q 2539.2 and random walk 2744.3. The single-branch ablation needs 581.6 steps. Success on unseen targets rises with more trained targets and closer targets. Fine-tuning scene-specific layers on new scenes converges faster as more training scenes are used. On a real SCITOS robot, sim-to-real fine-tuning converges 44% faster than training from scratch.
limitations: Main evaluation is on the same targets and scenes used for training. The scene-specific heads need scene identity and must be retrained for each new scene, so there is no zero-shot scene generalization; the single-branch model applied to new scenes is worse than chance.

Navigation happens in a coarse grid world (0.5 m steps, 90° turns) with small scenes and image goals. Generalization to new targets degrades with distance from trained targets, and results are mostly in figures rather than standardized metrics.
The real-robot test is small: 28 discrete locations, 2 targets (door, microwave), and it still requires training on real images.
